1.pericope_label: The proverbs of Solomon the son of David, king of Israel

schools.summary: Delitzsch reports that the ancients took the superscription to make the whole book Solomon's, gives the book's length as eight hundred verses, and records the rabbinic device of dividing each verse in two to reconcile that with the three thousand proverbs; Ellicott explains the book's character from the peace of Solomon's reign, which favoured a sententious philosophy where David's wars had called forth impassioned eloquence.

Gill counts the verses twice, with and without the first nine chapters which he treats as introduction, notes that neither figure approaches a third of the three thousand, and derives the Hebrew name from a root carrying both similitude and dominion.

Clarke thinks it very likely Solomon composed only part and collected the rest, defends that against the charge of derogating from the book's authority, traces proverbial wisdom outward to every ancient nation, and appends a five-part division of the book, a chronology, a note on the liberties of the Greek version, and a description of an illuminated manuscript on his own shelf.

Henry takes the proverbs as Solomon's own and inspired, distinguishes them from the three thousand his servants collected, and reads his father's troubled life and his own quiet reign as the reason one wrote devotion and the other instruction.

debates.question: Did Solomon compose all these proverbs?

positions.view: They are his own writing and divinely inspired, distinct from the collected three thousand.
Very likely he did not compose them all, but gathered what agreed with the Spirit of truth; whatever truth is found among men came originally from God.
The ancients read the superscription as making the whole book his.

debates.question: How long is the book, and how does that square with the three thousand proverbs?

positions.view: Six hundred and fifty-nine verses without the introductory chapters, nine hundred and fifteen with them, not a third of the three thousand.
Eight hundred verses, the difference met by the rabbinic suggestion that each verse divides in two.

outliers.note: Argues from chronology that Solomon preceded every famous Gentile moralist by centuries and so could owe them nothing, which sits awkwardly beside his own concession that Solomon collected from heathens.
Regrets that Solomon's natural history of trees, beasts, fowls and fishes is wholly lost, and would exchange the three surviving books for it.

themes: The proverbs of Solomon the son of David, king of Israel;

2.pericope_label: To know wisdom and instruction; to perceive the words of understanding... To understand a proverb, and the interpretation; the words of the wise, and their dark sayings

schools.summary: Delitzsch sets out the structure by which the opening aim is expanded through the following verses, traces the first governing word to a root meaning to be firm, and explains the mongrel plural form of the word for the simple; Ellicott renders the same root as firmness, corrects the second word to discipline, and gives the phrase for wise counsels its literal sense of arts of seamanship.

Gill widens the purpose to ethics, politics and economics together and finally to the knowledge of Christ, finds similitude and dominion in the one root, and answers the promise of subtlety by appeal to the serpent and the dove.

Clarke widens the two governing words to the whole of heavenly teaching, traces the decay of the English word simple through four stages, and distinguishes two Hebrew words usually derived from one root; Wesley divides the wisdom briefly into human and divine.

debates.question: What does the word rendered instruction mean?

positions.view: Discipline, the knowledge of how to keep oneself under control.
The teaching that discovers all the parts of wisdom.
Instruction delivered either by God or by men toward the attainment of wisdom.
Wise and prudent instruction, especially Christ's own.

debates.question: Who are the simple, and is the subtlety promised them a good thing?

positions.view: Men open to good impressions who are also easily led astray; the Hebrew for subtlety is elsewhere used for guile, but here means the wisdom of serpents.
Men of weak capacity who may reach a serpentine subtlety while remaining harmless as doves.
The unwary and precipitate; the English word has decayed from plain dealing to foolishness for want of honesty in the world.
One whose heart stands open to every influence, a term that may go either way but usually goes the worse.

outliers.note: Devotes his longest note here to the decay of the English word simple, and blames its degradation on the rarity of plain dealing.
Derives the word for a dark saying from a root meaning twisted, speech turned aside rather than open, and connects it with the word for a mocker as one who uses oblique words.

themes: To know wisdom and instruction; to perceive the words of understanding;
To receive the instruction of wisdom, justice, and judgment, and equity;
To give subtilty to the simple, to the young man knowledge and discretion.
A wise man will hear, and will increase learning; and a man of understanding shall attain unto wise counsels:
To understand a proverb, and the interpretation; the words of the wise, and their dark sayings.

7.pericope_label: The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge: but fools despise wisdom and instruction... For they shall be an ornament of grace unto thy head, and chains about thy neck

schools.summary: Delitzsch calls the verse the book's motto and notes that the Hebrew for beginning means both the point one starts from and the basis one stands on; Ellicott counts the phrase thirteen times in the book, and alone treats the fear of the Lord as superseded by a higher motive under the new covenant.
Gill rules out a servile fear of punishment and insists on a filial fear presupposing knowledge of God as a father, and observes that Solomon proceeds in the order of the ten commandments.

Clarke defines the fear as the reverence owed a Creator, then expounds religion itself as the two commandments, and turns the ornament into a maxim about the road to civil eminence; Wesley compresses the fear to reverence and obedience.

Henry unpacks the motto three ways, notes that a pagan philosopher's verses open with the same two rules in corrupted form, and observes that the divine law secures the mother's honour where Gentile codes secured only the father's.

debates.question: Is the fear of the Lord the highest motive?

positions.view: It is the beginning and also the centre, the alpha and omega of knowledge.
It is filial rather than servile, and takes in the whole of religious worship.
It may be the beginning of wisdom, but something better is to be aimed at, since he that feareth is not made perfect in love.
It is the reverence every intelligent being owes his Creator, and inseparable from love, since without love there is no obedience.

debates.question: Who are the fools that despise wisdom?

positions.view: Atheists who set God at defiance.
Evil men, of bad hearts, heads and ways.
Self-willed persons who will listen to no advice.
Wicked men who despise the very means of getting wisdom.

outliers.note: Treats the book's own motto as belonging to a superseded dispensation, the fear of the Lord giving way to the love of God under the new covenant.
Infers from the father's absence at work and the mother's presence at home that she is the one who properly gives the household its laws.

themes: The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge: but fools despise wisdom and instruction.
My son, hear the instruction of thy father, and forsake not the law of thy mother:
For they shall be an ornament of grace unto thy head, and chains about thy neck.

10.pericope_label: My son, if sinners entice thee, consent thou not... So are the ways of every one that is greedy of gain; which taketh away the life of the owners thereof

schools.summary: Delitzsch reads the intensive form as men in whom sin has become habit, derives the verb for entice from a root meaning to open, counts three distinct arguments against joining them, and dismisses the reading that would make the net one strewn with bait; Ellicott takes the scene as brigandage, a crime the country's terrain and neighbours always invited, and numbers two reasons.
Gill limits the sinners to notorious offenders whose trade is sin, offers two readings of the bird and the net, and reads the ambush as recoiling on those who set it.

Clarke makes the answering verb the hinge, since the will can never be forced and God could not otherwise judge the world, enlarges the crime to a village destroyed, and ends by calling the covetous tradesman a murderer in God's sight; Wesley reads the recoil plainly.

Henry treats the highwaymen as a specimen of every enticement, traces the courtship from come with us to a shared purse, turns their precious substance against them, and presses that these men are worse than birds, since the fowler at least conceals his snare.

positions.view: Yes, a warning against a crime the country was always exposed to.
Yes, and the words are exactly what is spoken when such a gang forms.
A specimen only, standing for every evil into which sinners entice men.

debates.question: What does the proverb of the net and the bird mean?

positions.view: That a net spread in sight is spread in vain, so the seducers must work in secret.
Either that the innocent are taken without cause as a bird is, or that the bird is too intent on the corn to see the net.
That these men are worse than birds, since they see the end of their road and rush on regardless.
That their folly is the second reason against joining them, for the net they hid will take their own foot.

outliers.note: Turns the closing verse on his own readers, calling the tradesman who opens shop after shop to undersell his rivals a murderer in God's sight.
Hears in the phrase about swallowing men alive a deliberate allusion, in fact and in wording, to the fate of Korah's company.

themes: My son, if sinners entice thee, consent thou not.
If they say, Come with us, let us lay wait for blood, let us lurk privily for the innocent without cause:
Let us swallow them up alive as the grave; and whole, as those that go down into the pit:
We shall find all precious substance, we shall fill our houses with spoil:
Cast in thy lot among us; let us all have one purse:
My son, walk not thou in the way with them; refrain thy foot from their path:
For their feet run to evil, and make haste to shed blood.
Surely in vain the net is spread in the sight of any bird.
And they lay wait for their own blood; they lurk privily for their own lives.
So are the ways of every one that is greedy of gain; which taketh away the life of the owners thereof.

20.pericope_label: Wisdom crieth without; she uttereth her voice in the streets... How long, ye simple ones, will ye love simplicity? and the scorners delight in their scorning, and fools hate knowledge?

schools.summary: Delitzsch counts the fourfold statement that Wisdom preaches and preaches publicly, explains the chief place as the point from which streets divide, and marks a distinction of tense between the continuing love of the simple and the settled pleasure of the scorners; Ellicott alone shows his working, allowing that Solomon may have meant only a poetic description before arguing the case for the prophetic reading.
Gill rules out every alternative and identifies Wisdom directly with Christ, and turns the address on the Jews of the gospels.
Clarke holds that the personification means nothing beyond the teaching given by revelation or by the Spirit's voice in the heart; Wesley takes it as the wisdom of God revealed in his word.

Henry keeps every stage of the range at once, human understanding, civil government, revelation and Christ himself, and softens the reproof by noting that the question how long implies God desires conversion and not ruin.

debates.question: Who is the Wisdom that cries in the streets?

positions.view: Christ, since what is ascribed to Wisdom in this book belongs properly to a divine person.
Nothing beyond the teaching given to man by revelation or by the Spirit's voice in the heart.
The wisdom of God revealed in his word.
All of these at once, from conscience and civil government up to Christ, who both pleads and sentences here.
Perhaps originally a poetic description of the godly, but rightly held prophetic from the earliest Christian times.

debates.question: How are the three classes addressed to be characterized?

positions.view: By their roots: the accessible, the twisters of words, and the mentally coarse.
Historically, the name for the scorners first appearing when prosperity favoured scepticism.
The scorners are the worst of sinners and those who hate knowledge the worst of fools.
The Jews of the gospels, the simple being those first called by Christ and despised as unlearned.

outliers.note: Sets out his reasoning for the christological reading rather than asserting it, arguing from a saying attributed to the wisdom of God in one gospel and spoken by Christ in another.
Observes that Wisdom names only the simple in her address, expecting to find access to them soonest.

themes: Wisdom crieth without; she uttereth her voice in the streets:
She crieth in the chief place of concourse, in the openings of the gates: in the city she uttereth her words, saying,
How long, ye simple ones, will ye love simplicity? and the scorners delight in their scorning, and fools hate knowledge?

23.pericope_label: Turn you at my reproof: behold, I will pour out my spirit unto you, I will make known my words unto you... But whoso hearkeneth unto me shall dwell safely, and shall be quiet from fear of evil

schools.summary: Delitzsch argues that the opening clause is conditional and not a wish, marks the pause at which Wisdom turns from invitation to judgment, and reads the word for turning away as desertion rather than conversion; Ellicott refuses to take the laughter literally, since human folly can give God no pleasure, and glosses the prosperity as the apathy of those who cannot believe God will act.

Gill distinguishes the effectual internal call from the external call that may be refused, calls the laughter an anthropopathy while holding that God will delight in the glory of his justice, and refers the whole judgment to the destruction of Jerusalem by Rome.

Clarke confines the passage to robbers awaiting execution and denies it any application to the eternal state, reads the turning away as an accomplice turning king's evidence, and ends on the safety of the innocent man; Wesley widens the calling to ministers, judgments and conscience alike.

positions.view: The destruction of the Jewish nation by the Romans.
The execution of condemned robbers in this life only; nothing here applies to the eternal state, and no penitent is ever refused while life lasts.
The final shutting of the door by the master of the house on those who would not call while he was near.

debates.question: What is the turning away of the simple?

positions.view: Apostasy, the word carrying desertion rather than conversion, so that turning from wisdom and from God are one.
Turning away from God, their very prosperity making them presumptuous.
The aversion of the Jews to Christ; or, on another reading, the false rest of the simple who cry peace when destruction is at hand.
An accomplice turning king's evidence against his own gang while they are still secure in their spoil.

outliers.note: Explicitly refuses the eschatological reading of the passage that the other voices assume, insisting that life is the time of probation and no penitent is ever refused within it.
Denies that the divine laughter can be literal, since the sight of human folly gives God no pleasure, and reduces it to acting as if he mocked.

themes: Turn you at my reproof: behold, I will pour out my spirit unto you, I will make known my words unto you.
Because I have called, and ye refused; I have stretched out my hand, and no man regarded;
But ye have set at nought all my counsel, and would none of my reproof:
I also will laugh at your calamity; I will mock when your fear cometh;
When your fear cometh as desolation, and your destruction cometh as a whirlwind; when distress and anguish cometh upon you.
Then shall they call upon me, but I will not answer; they shall seek me early, but they shall not find me:
For that they hated knowledge, and did not choose the fear of the Lord:
They would none of my counsel: they despised all my reproof.
Therefore shall they eat of the fruit of their own way, and be filled with their own devices.
For the turning away of the simple shall slay them, and the prosperity of fools shall destroy them.
But whoso hearkeneth unto me shall dwell safely, and shall be quiet from fear of evil.
